trade-world-economy-s1.title: What one day of work can make in two countries

table.caption: Output of one day of work (invented data for practice). Each country can make one good or the other.

map.label: Reference map of Latin America with the four founding members of Mercosur shaded: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, in the south and east of South America
map.legendTitle: Founding members of Mercosur (Treaty of Asunción, 1991)

items.q: According to the table, which country has the absolute advantage in making tablets?
options: Country F, because tablets cost it less coffee
Country E, because it makes 6 tablets to F's 4
Neither, because the two make the same number
Both, because each can make tablets

why.correct: Absolute advantage compares output: in one day E makes 6 tablets and F makes 4.
options: That is the test for comparative advantage, not absolute advantage.
Right: absolute advantage means making more with the same work: 6 against 4.
E makes 6 tablets a day and F makes 4, so they differ.
Absolute advantage goes to the country that makes more, here E.

items.q: In Country E, what is the opportunity cost of making one tablet, in bags of coffee?

why.correct: In one day E can make 12 bags of coffee or 6 tablets, so one tablet costs $\frac{12}{6} = 2$ bags of coffee.

mistakes.why: That is the cost of one bag of coffee in tablets (0.5). For one tablet, divide the coffee given up (12) by the tablets made (6).
That is Country F's cost (1 bag). Use Country E's row: 12 bags or 6 tablets.

items.q: Which country has the comparative advantage in making tablets?
options: Country E, because it makes more tablets
Neither, because E is better at both goods
Country F: a tablet costs it 1 bag, not 2
Both, because each country makes some tablets

why.correct: A tablet costs E 2 bags of coffee ($\frac{12}{6}$) and F 1 bag ($\frac{4}{4}$). The lower opportunity cost is F's, so F has the comparative advantage in tablets and E in coffee.
options: That is absolute advantage. Compare opportunity costs: a tablet costs E 2 bags of coffee but costs F 1 bag.
Being better at both gives E absolute advantage in both, but each country still has a comparative advantage in one good.
Right: F gives up less coffee for each tablet, so F has the comparative advantage in tablets.
Only one country can have the lower opportunity cost of a good.

items.q: If each country specializes by comparative advantage and they trade, what is the likely outcome?
options: E makes coffee, F tablets; both gain
E makes both goods, and F stops producing
F makes coffee, E makes tablets, and both gain
Neither gains

why.correct: E has the comparative advantage in coffee (a bag costs it half a tablet) and F in tablets (a tablet costs it 1 bag), so specializing and trading leaves both better off.
options: Right: specializing in the good with the lower opportunity cost and trading lets both consume more.
That follows absolute advantage, and it ignores the gain from F's lower cost for tablets.
This swaps the advantages: E gives up less to make coffee, F gives up less to make tablets.
Gains come from differences in opportunity cost, which exist here.

items.q: The shaded countries agreed in 1991 to lower tariffs on trade among themselves. What kind of organization did they form?
options: A trade bloc
A cartel of oil exporters, like OPEC
A lender to governments, like the IMF
A microlending network for small firms

why.correct: Lowering tariffs among a group of member countries makes a trade bloc.
options: Right: a group of countries that lowers or removes tariffs among its members is a trade bloc.
OPEC sets oil output; Mercosur lowers tariffs among its members.
The IMF lends to governments; it does not cut tariffs among a few members.
Microlending gives small loans to people, not tariff cuts among countries.

items.q: At what scale of analysis does this map show Mercosur?
options: Local: one city and its suburbs
National: a single country's provinces
Regional: several countries
Global: the whole world

why.correct: The data are four countries in one world region, so the scale is regional.
options: Four whole countries are shaded, far more than one city.
Four countries are shown, not the inside of one.
Right: four countries in South America make a regional scale.
Only Latin America is shown.

items.q: What is the most likely effect of Mercosur on trade between Brazil and Argentina?
options: It falls
It grows, as tariffs between them fall
It stops, as each buys from outside the bloc instead
It does not change, because tariffs do not affect prices

why.correct: Cutting tariffs among members lowers the price of their goods to each other, so trade inside the bloc tends to grow.
options: Members lower tariffs on each other, which encourages trade.
Right: lower tariffs make each other's goods cheaper, so trade between members grows.
The bloc favors trade inside it, not outside.
A tariff raises the price of imports, so cutting it changes trade.

items.q: Why might a member country give up some control of its own trade policy by joining a bloc like the one on the map?
options: The bloc forbids members from trading with outsiders
Members agree on shared tariff rules
The IMF takes over its budget when it joins
Members swap their national currencies with Japan

why.correct: A trade bloc is supranational: members agree on shared rules, trading some sovereignty over trade policy for access to a larger market.
options: The point of a bloc is more trade, not less.
Right: the bloc sets common rules, so a member gives up some freedom to set its own tariffs in return for wider access to markets.
Joining a trade bloc does not hand a budget to the IMF.
Nothing about Mercosur involves Japan's currency.

items.q: Costa Rica grows bananas in its warm lowlands, and Canada grows wheat and makes machines. Trade between them shows which idea most directly?
options: Complementarity: each supplies a need
Absolute advantage in each good for Canada
A tariff on bananas entering Canada
Structural adjustment by the IMF in Costa Rica

why.correct: Complementarity exists when one place supplies what another needs, here because the two climates differ.
options: Right: one place's supply meets another's need, largely because of climate.
Canada cannot grow bananas well, so it lacks an advantage in them.
Nothing in the example is about a tax on imports.
Nothing in the example involves an IMF loan.

items.q: A country puts a 25% tariff on imported steel. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Imports cost more, so home steelmakers sell more
Imported steel gets cheaper, so imports rise
Steel-selling countries remove their own tariffs
Home steel prices fall as competition grows

why.correct: A tariff is a tax on imports: imported steel costs more, which helps home steelmakers but raises costs for buyers and may bring tariffs in return.
options: Right: the tariff raises import prices, which protects home producers, though buyers pay more.
A tariff is a tax on imports, so it makes them cost more.
Other countries are more likely to answer with tariffs of their own.
A tariff reduces foreign competition, so home prices tend to rise.

items.q: In the 1980s, many Latin American governments sold state-owned companies, cut spending and lowered tariffs. Which idea do these policies reflect?
options: Dependency theory
Complementarity
Neoliberalism
Commodity dependence

why.correct: Selling state firms, cutting spending and opening trade are neoliberal policies, which spread after the 1982 debt crisis.
options: Dependency theory would favor less reliance on trade with the core, not lower tariffs.
Complementarity explains why two places trade; it is not a set of government policies.
Right: shrinking the government's role, selling state firms and freeing trade are neoliberal policies.
That describes relying on one export, not a set of policies.

items.q: After Mexico said in 1982 that it could not pay its foreign debts, the IMF lent money on the condition of structural adjustment. Which gives both sides of the effects?
options: It ended the debt, and each group gained
It cut tariffs to zero, and nobody lost work
It closed Mexico's economy to trade, raising prices
It restored trust, but cuts hurt clinics

why.correct: Structural adjustment loans came with spending cuts, sales of state firms and open markets: supporters say they restored stability, critics say they hurt public services.
options: Debt did not vanish, and critics point to real losers from spending cuts.
Opening markets cost some protected firms and workers their jobs.
Structural adjustment opened economies to trade; it did not close them.
Right: supporters credit it with restoring trust and growth; critics say spending cuts fell on the poorest.

items.q: What does the World Trade Organization (WTO) do?
options: Lends to governments in a debt crisis
Sets trade rules and settles disputes
Sets how much oil its members pump
Measures the Human Development Index

why.correct: The WTO writes the rules of trade among its members, pushes for lower tariffs and settles trade disputes.
options: That is the IMF.
Right: since 1995 the WTO has set rules for trade among its members and settled their disputes.
That is OPEC.
The UNDP publishes the HDI.

items.q: A US state offers a carmaker free land and ten years of lower taxes to build a plant there. How does this compare with a national tariff on imported cars?
options: Both are government steps to win jobs, at different scales
Both are trade blocs among several countries
The state offer is neoliberal and the tariff is not a policy
Both are loans from the IMF to the carmaker

why.correct: Governments at every scale shape where industry goes: a state uses incentives to win a plant, while a national tariff protects a whole industry.
options: Right: the state acts at a regional scale to attract one plant; a tariff acts at the national scale for a whole industry.
Neither involves an agreement among countries.
A tariff is a policy; the difference is scale and method.
Neither is an IMF loan; the IMF lends to governments.

items.q: In 2008, a crisis that began with risky home loans in the United States spread to banks, trade and jobs around the world. What does this show?
options: The world economy is interdependent
Tariffs block crises at borders
The crisis stayed at the local scale
Periphery countries caused the crisis

why.correct: Financial and trade links make economies interdependent, so a crisis in one large economy spreads worldwide.
options: Right: banks, trade and investment link places, so trouble in one country spreads.
The crisis crossed borders through banks and trade.
It spread from one country to the global scale.
It began with home loans in the United States.

items.q: Which of these are trade blocs? Select all that apply.
options: The European Union
Mercosur
The International Monetary Fund
The Grameen Bank
The UN Development Programme

why.correct: The EU and Mercosur cut trade barriers among their members; the IMF, Grameen Bank and UNDP are not trade blocs.
options: Right: its members trade freely with each other.
Right: its members cut tariffs among themselves.
The IMF lends to governments; it does not cut tariffs among members.
It is a microlending bank in Bangladesh.
The UNDP publishes the HDI and works on development; it is not a trade bloc.

items.q: Build an explanation of which good Country F (in the coffee and tablets table) should make, using the right kind of advantage.

why.correct: Comparative advantage goes to the lower opportunity cost: F gives up 1 bag of coffee per tablet, E gives up 2.

specific.frame: Country F has the ___ in ___ because ___, so it should make them and trade.
specific.model: Country F has the comparative advantage in tablets because a tablet costs it only 1 bag of coffee while it costs Country E 2 bags, so it should make them and trade.

concept.label: Kind of advantage
options: comparative advantage
absolute advantage

why.1: F makes fewer tablets than E, so it has no absolute advantage; its advantage is the lower opportunity cost.

outcome.label: Good
options: tablets
coffee

why.1: A bag of coffee costs F 1 tablet but E only half a tablet, so E has the advantage in coffee.

cause.label: Because
options: a tablet costs it only 1 bag of coffee while it costs Country E 2 bags
it makes more tablets than Country E

why.1: F makes 4 tablets to E's 6; the reason is the lower opportunity cost.

items.q: Using the coffee and tablets table (Country E: 12 bags or 6 tablets a day; Country F: 4 bags or 4 tablets), place the good each country should specialize in.

slips.why: E has the absolute advantage in both, but trade follows comparative advantage: E gives up less to make coffee.
A tablet costs E 2 bags of coffee but F only 1, so F has the comparative advantage in tablets.

why.correct: A bag of coffee costs E half a tablet and F one tablet, so E makes coffee; a tablet costs F one bag and E two, so F makes tablets.
